title: Australia to Bar Most Student Visa Holders From Bringing Families in Migration Crackdown
excerpt: Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke unveiled the restrictions on Thursday as part of a broader overhaul targeting net migration of 225,000 by 2028 — a direct hit to the A$53.6 billion international education sector that depends heavily on Indian students.
body:
• Most international students will lose the right to bring partners and children to Australia; PhD candidates and students from some Pacific and Southeast Asian nations are exempt.
  • Student visa renewals will require progression to a higher qualification, working holiday extensions move to a ballot, and all visitor visas will carry a "no further stay" condition.
  • The government is targeting net migration of 225,000 by 2028, down from about 300,000 now and a 518,000 peak in 2023.
  • The rules hit Indian students hard — families are a common part of the Australia study plan — though existing dependent arrangements already on visas are not automatically revoked.

Australia will bar most international students from bringing their partners and children with them while they study, Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke announced on Thursday, unveiling the sharpest immigration turn of Canberra's Labor government — and one that will force many Indian students to rethink plans built around relocating as a family.

Under the measures, family members will no longer be permitted on most student visa arrangements. PhD candidates and students from some Pacific Island countries and Southeast Asian nations will retain the ability to bring partners and children under specified arrangements. Currently, spouses and partners of international students can accompany them and may work, while dependent children under 18 can also be brought.

The new rules

The overhaul extends well beyond students. Working holiday visa holders seeking to extend their stay will face a new ballot system, replacing the current extension arrangements that agriculture and tourism employers rely on. All visitor visas will carry a "no further stay" provision, meaning holders will generally not be able to remain in Australia while applying for another visa category, including a partner visa.

Students will also face additional conditions when renewing student visas: they will generally need to progress to a higher qualification level. Burke framed this as a crackdown on "visa hopping" — the practice of finishing one course and switching to another, sometimes at what he described as "not-so-legitimate educational providers," to extend a stay.

"If you want to come on a temporary basis to Australia, apply for a temporary visa. If you want to come to Australia permanently, apply for a permanent visa. And if you no longer have a valid visa, you should leave Australia."

— Tony Burke, Home Affairs Minister

Enforcement is being stepped up in parallel. The government will recruit 100 additional compliance officers to deal with people who remain after their visas expire, and officials are examining whether a Melbourne quarantine facility used during the COVID-19 pandemic can be repurposed to accommodate immigration detainees.

Context and background

The government expects the package to push annual net migration down to roughly 225,000 by 2028 — close to pre-pandemic levels — from about 300,000 now, with an interim target of 245,000 in the current financial year. The numbers have already been falling: net overseas migration totalled 306,000 in the year to June 30, 2025, down from 429,000 in 2024 and a peak of 518,000 in 2023. Government figures show 337,427 student visas were granted in 2025-26, including 45,991 issued to dependants or family members.

The announcement landed days after the hard-right One Nation party, which has been surging in the polls, proposed slashing temporary migration by 750,000 over three years to give Australians "breathing space," with a longer-term aim of restricting net migration to 130,000. Burke rejected any suggestion the measures were politically motivated: "It's simply demonstrably wrong to suspect that somehow this is a recent bit of work done to deal with a political climate — it's not," he told reporters. According to Australian Associated Press, Burke's National Press Club speech had been shelved six weeks earlier amid cabinet disagreement, and he conceded the final package was less comprehensive than he wanted after negotiations with the coalition broke down — leaving him with regulatory tweaks rather than legislative changes.

The business community has already pushed back, warning that curbs on working holiday visas — a measure even One Nation did not propose — will hurt agriculture and tourism. Migration remains one of the top concerns for voters alongside the cost of living, with critics arguing high intake has strained housing, infrastructure and social cohesion.

Impact on Indian students

The family restrictions land hardest on students from countries such as India, Nepal and Bangladesh, where applicants commonly plan to take a spouse or children with them. Indian students considering postgraduate and other higher-education programmes will now need to check whether their course falls under an exemption before making visa, accommodation and relocation decisions.

There is some reassurance for those already in the country: the reforms are focused on future visa arrangements, and Burke said existing family arrangements attached to visas will not be automatically revoked — meaning families already in Australia together will not automatically be separated.

The policy also collides with Australia's own economic interests. International education generated A$53.6 billion (about $38 billion) in the year to June 2025, making it the country's fourth-largest export. Universities and education-sector representatives have warned that restricting family members could make Australia less attractive relative to competitor destinations — a concern with real commercial weight given how heavily the sector depends on South Asian enrolments.

Australia is not moving alone, though its version is among the most sweeping. Britain barred most international students from bringing dependents from January 2024, with exceptions including postgraduate research students, and Canada tightened eligibility for spouses' open work permits from January 2025.

What's next

The changes arrive as regulatory tweaks rather than legislation, which may speed implementation but leaves the framework open to revision. Universities are expected to lobby for broader exemptions, particularly for postgraduate coursework students, and education agents in India will be recalculating advice for the 2027 intake season. Prospective students and their families should watch for the detailed regulations — especially the precise list of exempt countries and qualifications — before committing deposits or relocation plans.
image_caption: Australia is barring most student visa holders from bringing family members as part of a migration crackdown. The policy targets dependents of international students at Australian universities.
nri_angle: The restrictions hit a core diaspora pathway: Indian students, one of Australia's largest international-student cohorts, commonly relocate with spouses and children, and many will now have to choose between leaving family behind or picking another country.
